\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(D=\{d:d\mid 250\}\). The divisors are
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]

We first extract the structure forced by the condition
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j).
\]

Taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=i.
\]
If \(i\mid j\), then
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=i=|A_i|,
\]
so \(A_i\subseteq A_j\). Hence for all \(i,j\),
\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]

For each positive integer \(n\), define
\[
B_n=A_n\setminus \bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}}A_d.
\]
Because \(A_d\subseteq A_n\) whenever \(d\mid n\), the sets \(B_n\) are well-defined. We claim that for all \(m,n\),
\[
B_n\subseteq A_m \iff n\mid m.
\]
If \(n\mid m\), this follows from \(A_n\subseteq A_m\). If \(n\nmid m\), let \(g=\gcd(n,m)<n\). Then
\[
A_n\cap A_m=A_g,
\]
and \(B_n\) is disjoint from \(A_g\), so \(B_n\cap A_m=\varnothing\).

Thus for each \(m\),
\[
A_m=\bigsqcup_{n\mid m}B_n
\]
is a disjoint union. Therefore
\[
|A_m|=\sum_{n\mid m}|B_n|.
\]
Since \(|A_m|=m\) and \(\sum_{n\mid m}\varphi(n)=m\), Möbius inversion gives
\[
|B_n|=\varphi(n).
\]

So for the divisors of \(250\), we have disjoint blocks
\[
B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50},B_{125},B_{250}
\]
with sizes
\[
\varphi(d)\in\{1,1,4,4,20,20,100,100\},
\]
and
\[
B_e\subseteq A_d \iff e\mid d.
\]
The total number of elements in
\[
U=\bigcup_{d\mid 250}A_d=\bigcup_{d\mid 250}B_d
\]
is
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\varphi(d)=250.
\]

Now order the \(250\) elements of \(U\) by increasing label. For each \(d\mid 250\), let \(C_d\) be the position (rank) of the last element of \(B_d\) in this order. Then
\[
\max A_d\ge \max_{e\mid d} C_e.
\]
Also, if the \(250\) elements are relabeled consecutively in the same order, each block \(B_d\) would be consecutive, and its completion position would be the prefix sum of the block sizes. This can only decrease the above quantities. Hence it suffices to minimize, over all permutations of the eight blocks, the quantity
\[
S=\sum_{d\mid 250}\max_{e\mid d} C_e,
\]
where \(C_d\) is the completion time of block \(B_d\) after placing the blocks consecutively.

Let \(p_e=\varphi(e)\). For a permutation of the eight blocks, \(C_e\) is the prefix sum up to \(e\). We show that an optimal permutation is forced.

First, if a block \(f\) appears immediately before a divisor \(e\mid f\), swapping them does not increase \(S\). Indeed, if the time before \(f\) is \(t\), then before the swap
\[
C_f=t+p_f,\qquad C_e=t+p_f+p_e,
\]
and after the swap
\[
C_e=t+p_e,\qquad C_f=t+p_f+p_e.
\]
For any \(d\), if \(f\nmid d\), only possibly \(C_e\) decreases; if \(f\mid d\), then \(e\mid d\) and the new \(C_f\) equals the old \(C_e\), so the maximum over divisors of \(d\) is unchanged. Thus \(S\) does not increase. Repeating this eliminates all divisibility inversions, so an optimal order is a linear extension of the divisibility poset.

In a linear extension, every divisor \(e\mid d\) appears before \(d\), so
\[
\max_{e\mid d}C_d=C_d.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\sum_{d\mid 250}C_d.
\]

Now, within a linear extension, if two adjacent blocks \(i,j\) satisfy \(p_i>p_j\), then swapping them reduces \(\sum C_d\) by \(p_i-p_j\). This swap is valid because \(p_i>p_j\) implies \(i\nmid j\), and the order was already a linear extension. Repeating gives a linear extension with nondecreasing \(p_d\).

For our eight blocks,
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
\varphi(d)&1&1&4&4&20&20&100&100
\end{array}
\]
and the divisibility relations force the unique nondecreasing linear extension to be
\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;10,\;25,\;50,\;125,\;250.
\]
The corresponding completion times are
\[
1,\;2,\;6,\;10,\;30,\;50,\;150,\;250.
\]
Therefore every valid sequence satisfies
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
\ge
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

It remains to show \(499\) is attainable. Define disjoint sets \(B_d\) for \(d\mid 250\) as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(e\nmid 250\), choose \(B_e\) arbitrarily from labels larger than \(250\), with \(|B_e|=\varphi(e)\), so that all \(B_e\) are pairwise disjoint. Then define
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{e\mid n}B_e.
\]
Then
\[
|A_n|=\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)=n,
\]
and
\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{e\mid i,\ e\mid j}B_e
=\bigcup_{e\mid \gcd(i,j)}B_e
=A_{\gcd(i,j)},
\]
so \(|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)\).

For \(d\mid 250\), the maxima are exactly
\[
1,2,6,10,30,50,150,250,
\]
whose sum is \(499\). Hence the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}
\]
